segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This conversation with Helmer Ringsage took place at his home in Moscow on February 12th, 1976. The interviewer is Sam Schrager.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: My, uh, I was the oldest, and I'll tell you the words my mother told me when she was on her dying bed. I was just old enough to realize that she was dying, you know. And them days they claimed, I don't know why they did, but they kind of had the idea that the older one had to look after younger ones. Well, all the rest of them were the youngest. I was the oldest. And when she just, just before she took her last breath, she says, Helmer, she says, you're the oldest, you look after the children. And then she died, just that way. Boy, I never forgot it either. And so I did, I tried, you know, to help my, well, here's what happened. After mother died, see, well that Simon, the one that died with cancer, I'm telling you about, he was only a kid, seven years old. No, wait a minute, see now. No, he wasn't that old then, but I mean when he was cooking.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He was seven. No, he was only about four when she died. But he was cooking when he was seven. Well, later on, let's see, when he was seven, that would be about, he was born in, just a minute, he's seven years younger than I am, that would be 95 when he was born. Seven, now we figured out when he was seven, that would be 95. She died in 1901, now wait a minute. So he would have been six. He was six years old when she died. Well, I guess Dad learned him that year, so when he was seven, a year after that, he became the kind of the kitchen guy to look after things. Because we boys, our older boys, Steinert and I, when it come harvest time, I mean, we had to go out and do the shocking to them ..., see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was he, could he handle that at seven? Could he take care of the kitchen?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, he was a faithful guy. Dad depended on him. He could direct him and he was a wonderful kid. But that younger, and then, no, that wasn't the youngest, that was Julius. He was a mischievous little devil. He was our radio in the home. And he, one time, that was before Dad, let's see, yeah, that was before Dad got that house built, see. And we had, I'll show you the kitchen part, it's over there. He had a log house in this kitchen part on the back of that, and that's where Mother died in. Now, I had a cousin down here, of course, she lives here in Moscow. Her and her brother and his wife and her husband come up here one day to visit. That's my cousin, see. And she, I happened to mention that my mother died when she was not quite 31, or 32. She's just past 31. She's a young woman. And then she foolishly asked, you know, made me mad right away.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: She says, why didn't she live any longer?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, I said, come here, I'll show you what I showed her. You see that little, Dad used that for chicken house, little wands, board thickness of a bedroom, and a wood stove to heat it with. Now I said, I'd like to see you live in something like that and raise a family. That's what she, that last baby she had was born in that place. And her jumping on to me like that, her brother sat in there, and her husband, no, I didn't give a damn about it. For her asking, for her talking like that, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was your mother sick for, was it a long sickness?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, well, about a year. She had TB for about a whole year. And oh boy, she'd cough sometimes, you don't choke. You'd think she was going to pass out most any time. She pretty near dead. She'd choke and sit there and wheeze a long time before she'd get her breath, you know. Oh, she really suffered. But, and then to top it all, my wife got all sugar diabetes. But she was tough, she'd grade the family of four… here's my family… this is my wife. And I worked in the woods. And you see, I worked in the woods. This was taken in 1936, before any of them was married. This is my youngest daughter, she's the one who lives married, and she's got three daughters now. But there, she was eleven, and she was sixteen. Wait, no. Yeah, she was sixteen. And she was eighteen, and he was twenty. He was born in sixteen. And she was born in eighteen, and she was born in twenty.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And she wasn't born until nineteen twenty-five. She's five years younger than that. And my grandma, my Mrs., was forty-four, and I was thirty-six. I took a good picture there. Well, we all did. We got the hell of a good picture. It really is a good one. Anyway, I had work. You're saying you worked in the woods. That year I'd been up in the woods, saw on with a crosscut, see. And I had three partners. I tell you that, but that's what's kept me going. I've had good health, strength, and I guess the good Lord's been on my side all the time. I've had close calls, putting in to get killed, taking one eye up, and not this stuff. Oh yeah, I didn't tell you that. Then my brother Simon, the one that died with cancer, that's the first year I worked in the woods, nineteen hundred and twelve. And I was twenty-four years old. And so we had roped together, I guess. He was on the farm with Dad, but he was seventeen then.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: You see, I was seven years older. He was seventeen, I was twenty-four. But he's a big man then already. Good, husky man, and we always did get along good. So he wanted to get to work too, off the farm, see, in the winter. Long in the fall it was, after harvest field work was done. So I said, okay, he come up, and the first job we got was sawing out in the woods, falling timber. Well, it was both greenhorns, the first year, you see, we never knew a damn thing about it… well, of course, in them days they had what they call undercutter, to chop the undercut to fall your tree. And so,… my golly, well, and that's for a highland. I got a book, I'll show you that book, the camp I worked at. The kids, they bought it for me. I guess they located it somewhere. It's Bovill, close to the picture of Bovill, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Which camp was that?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, that was Camp Eight. Oh, I know about that one.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That was right near Collins there, right?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, it was about, I don't remember, it was kind of south east of Bovill.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, okay, so, but you had to cut this tree down?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, we had to cut, I was going to tell you about that. I was cutting these, he and Simon and I was following this timber, see. And, well, this undercutter couldn't keep us going, because we was cutting them, you cut them forty foot logs, and one of them swedes, they filed them saws good, and there's a white pine to saw, and god, we just about walked the tailbone off that poor guy. So, all he had to do was undercut and mark the log. We didn't have to mark, we just went along and cut them off, see. God damn, we shouldn't have done it. We only got two and a half a day. Six bits for gold a day. But, dammit, we were just interacting, and we enjoyed it. And, we was getting good feeding camp, you know, Potlatch Lumber Company fed good, so that we was full of pistol pittagers, you call it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you put in a ten hour day then?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Ten hours, boy! For two and a half, two bits a day, two bits an hour. And so, in a way, then, well, then it got, so, well, I, here's the deal. I applied for a job at the landing. I didn't want to stay out in the woods all winter, see. God damn snow would get pretty bad. So, I figured it'd be a little nicer down there, and I told my brother, Simon, he's a young kid, only seventeen, I said, Simon, I said, you better get a job in the kitchen, you're waiting on the tables for the lumberjacks. And, he wouldn't get so much a day, but he got so much a month, forty dollars. I said, that'll be better for you. Yeah, okay, he agreed. And that's the way we worked it. We went down there to where there's a donkey, I'll show you that pretty soon. And, and, I was loading, I mean, no, I wasn't loading. They had a top loader, stand on the car, load, placing these logs. And there's two guys, them days, now they got one big grapple fork, or, tongs they call them, to load. Them days, it was just a crotch chain, with a hook, two men, one at each end of the log. Well, this first hoistman that we had at camp eight, he was darn good.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He drank like a fish, but he was sober enough to do his work good. So, then, by golly, it went on and on and on.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you switch?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: It didn't long, fine and dandy, but Simon, my brother, you see, was in the kitchen doing good.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So, what was you doing?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, I was doing one, I was one of them that was doing the hooking. Another guy, not Simon, my brother, he got into the kitchen, see. So, then I, that was fine, we got along fine with that guy, see. And, pretty soon, Gil Pippen was our foreman. One-eyed, old, big, Irishman, I guess, and he weighed around 250. And, by God, he wanted to move us down to another setting, and that was just a young kid, 16 years old, doing the hoisting. And, that son of a bitch, he'd get reckless, see, he'd bring that log up a ways, and then he'd jerk it. And, the cotch changed the fly ring to fly ever which wing. Oh, God, we all three just decided we'd quit. Top loader and I and the other hooker. Dangerous. If we didn't get back to our original hoister.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That'd be dangerous.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, it was! God damn, they just put near got us. So, we got back to camp. Old Gil, well, he said he couldn't fire that kid, he said his dad was a good cook. Well, that's what, he had a good, sounded like a good reason. Well, alright, we said we was gonna quit. By God, we did quit, we didn't fool, we quit. And, I went there forever. Now, that's the story I wanted to get you, I'm gonna tell you. I got to Elk River, my brother still stayed in the kitchen. I told him, I said, you better stay there, you're inside. And, I said, that's a good, fine place for you. But, I said, I'm going to Elk River, trying to get a job in the mill. See, they run the mill there at Elk River. And, sure enough, I got there and I got a job, alright. But, I didn't get what I wanted, I wanted to be a fireman. You know, them days they had, they didn't have electricity in Elk River.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: They had to use dynamos, and them dynamos was fed with this sawdust from these, them big boilers was fed with this sawdust, see, at weekends. Weekends, they had to fire them, I had to fire them when I got the job. I didn't, wait now. You wanted a job. I wanted that job, see, they said, well, wait till somebody gets drunk. In them days, they had a lot of guys getting drunk. They had good whiskey, you know. And, they said, well, I tell you, if you'll take a job sweeping the floor down here with a jab, till we get a drunk guy, then by golly, we'll put you on. And, sure enough, wasn't about a week, I guess, that I had to sweep that floor down there. And, then I got this other job and they said, well, I said, well, I said, what am I going to do during the week? Oh, I said, ten pump. And, that was, say, that's the time I had to work twelve hours, night shift, twelve from six to six.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And, by golly, and I couldn't afford, I only got three, see, how much is that? Yeah, that's only two bits an hour, three dollars for that twelve hours.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How many days a week did you work?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, well, I had to work every day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Seven days a week?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, you see, because, well, not all day, no, I mean, I was firing them boilers Friday night, Saturday night, and Sunday night. Three nights. Rest of the time, I had a ten pump. I didn't have no weekends on. But, I wasn't carried on satisfied, I was young, I was only twenty-four. The kid, well, then pretty soon my brother wrote me. He said, the cooks are getting drunk. Said, I'll tell you, going, oh, he said, I don't like to stay here, he wrote and told me. Well, I felt sorry for him, I knew he wanted to work. And, I thought, by golly, I'll try and get a job out in the camp then… so, I did… i got a job out, what they call, C, Camp C, out of Alp River. And, that was what they called, bullcaw, you cut logs and split up wood for the cook car and for the campers, I mean, loggers. And, by golly, you know, they give us wet wood, wet white pine, we worked our heads off. Well, it was up to two o'clock in the morning trying to get that, get all them fires going. We had to get the heart of the wood that was any good at all for cooking with them. They burnt that in the cook stove scene. You had to keep the cooks going whether you got the bunk fires going or not. And, we used coal oil to start them, but, God, it was, you know what wet wood will do. Well, by God, we stayed there, I don't remember, about a week or two. And, we got fed up. I told the boss, I said, for God's sake, I just get somebody else. And, I told Simon, I said, you better go on home back to farm, I said.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So, he'd come out with you to work on that.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, he'd come over there, you see, and got on this job. Two of you was working. He was already on the job with me when we quit. And, I said, uh.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You were working, two of you worked together?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, yeah, we did. We had to saw that wood together, you see, just like we did when it was falling trees.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the pay on that job?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Same, two bits an hour. He was probably working. Well, it wasn't that because we worked, I think it was two and a half a day. And, we had to work half of the night or sometimes damn near all night to keep the fire to the goal. That's what got us disgusted.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, did you have no chance to sleep or anything?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, we'd sleep maybe from ten till two or three o'clock in the morning, three, four, five hours, something like that. Oh, it was rough.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So, you told him to go back to the farm?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Ah, he finally did. Well, we both quit. You see, we stayed, as I said, a couple, I don't remember now, but it may be a couple of weeks. Because, you had to give them time to get somebody else if you could. Because, if you wanted to respect the company, you had to kind of give them a little time ahead so you could come back and get a job the next year. That's what I realized. Well, so I told my brother, now I said we quit here. And I said, you go home. And I said, I had worked, I didn't tell you that. I had worked for the vet, veterinary, Potlatch veterinary in old Doc Palmer. Previous. Previous, in the fall, when I first come there. See, before I got into the woods at all. And, so I come back there, I knew him and my aunt, this Ed Swenson's brother's wife, see, he got killed by a tree one time.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: When he was sawing, that was down by Deary, Idaho.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Ed Swenson's brother?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, Isaac was his name. And she was living there in Boulder, taking in washing from these lumberjacks. And I felt sorry for her, and I said, well, you know, I said, if I can board with you, I'll pay you a board, the best I can. And she's just glad to get somebody and make a few dollars. He had a lot of little kids. He had this cousin living in Detroit, now Carl Swenson.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now, you know whether you've met him?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yes, sure. Yeah. Well, it was him, and then it was, let's see, Ernest and Dolph. And I guess, well, Oscar, that was her older son. He was working in camp. He was old enough to have a job in camp. But these other, let's see, it was Carl and Dolph and Ernest, three boys, and a girl named Idie. Bought four of them. She had four yet at home. She was supporting.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you know how it happened that he was killed?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, yeah, I bet. And that got me to lurk. When I went to the woods, boy, I become pretty catty about watching trees fall.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was he?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And I, God damn, I didn't tell you that. I'll tell you that accident when I and Simon was gone after a bit. I'll tell you that. Okay, I'll... Isaac had died.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was he right in Deary when that happened to him?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, yeah. They had a little forty acre place there in Deary then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was he working for the Potlatch or for himself?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, I was Potlatch company up. And, in a way, he, she, I had to sleep, God, it was cold that winter. All the job I got when I come back to the duck pond was hauling hay and when I got through with that, he said, well, he says, all I got now is snow shoveling for the sleigh hauler. See, they'd haul logs on great big bumps just like putting it like a truck. They'd have one team on it and they'd sand the roads so they wouldn't go too fast and going down these mountains, see. And, so, he said, I had asked for a job for teaming but I was glad I didn't get it. Well, they told me I couldn't handle it and I knew I couldn't.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What, a job for what?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: To drive a team on that sleigh haul. But, he gave me this job, a snow shovel, see, after. I stayed right through Clear to Spring.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now, where was this at?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Bovill, right in Bovill. And, so, in a way, I stayed there and, like I said, it was as cold as 22 below zero and seven foot of snow. Oh, I didn't tell you how we got, how lucky we, my brother and I were that we moved out of Elk River. The snow snowed till it blocked, there was no railroad traffic, no nothing in Elk River. It snowed 13 or 14 feet, they said, clear up over to the upstairs windows. My uncle, Adolph Swenson, that picture, I think my cousin still got in, shows a picture of that snow. Well, we just got out the day before, I think it was a day or so, not over two days after we got out of there till that happened.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So, what happened? Was all the people stuck there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, God, they were all, they were really sunk till they, no snow plows like they got now. No doggone tractors, nothing. They just had to wait till it just, well, I suppose the way they, I don't know how they did to get supplies in, but they had to move and over somewhere. The railroad couldn't get in yet. Well, probably the railroad did have snow plows on front that they could get out eventually. But God, it took quite a while, you know, that 13 feet of snow dropping down. Oh, God, it was about four or five feet when we left camp up there. And when we got to, I was more than that because, hell, it was seven feet in Bovill when I got there. And it stayed, it just kept snowing, kept snowing all winter. I'll tell you, that year, the snow didn't leave till owling May… in Park… god knows when it left in the woods.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, listen, when you, now you were working, you were working the snow shoveling you'd done in Bovill. That was for the sleigh hall?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That is for the sleigh hall, yeah. In 19, that was, well, that would be 1913, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Can you tell me how your aunt made do without her husband? Did she have any?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, she'd know. She had to take in washing. She charged so much of the shirt and ironed them and bended them. She was a working hunk. Say, that woman lived to be 97 years old right down here at the home in Lewiston. Oh, she was a husky. But the poor thing, she married again and was married 50 years with her second husband. A fellow named Carl, wait a minute, Carl Carlson. Or Charlie Carlson, they called him. I guess his name was Carl, but they had to change it to Charlie because this boy of hers was named Carl, see. I think that's the way it was. Well, anyway. So, she did remarry. That probably made it a lot easier. Oh, yeah. He had a little farm on Texas Ridge. So, they had, and he was a carpenter. Hell of a good carpenter. So, he was making pretty good living for her. That was a relief to her, you know. But then her kids were grown up too by that time, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And so, this Carl, down here to Lewiston, I'll say that much for him. He's the only one of them boys that really honored his mother. He seemed to it that she had money. After he got big enough, I mean, to work out, he'd always bring her stuff to eat before she married this other man. And not only that, when they finally sold their farm up there and moved to Lewiston, Charlie, he was a carpenter, of course, and he built a house. I don't know if he, no, I guess he bought the house, but he remodeled it. Made it handy for her, see. And all. But here's the deal, the way she got hurt. She was taking a bath and she sat down on the edge of the tub and slid off and fell and hurt her side. And they had to put her in the house, yeah, in the home. And there she stayed and stayed and stayed till she finally got so she couldn't realize things. She talked, but she didn't seem to realize hardly what she was saying. Poor girl. And I went down there and visited her several times. Carl always, when she could, understand why he was there and treating her, you know. And always on her birthday, he'd bring her a birthday cake or treat, see. And so did I, I gave her cards and stuff, you know. And she was, well, she had cooked, I didn't tell you that, after mother died. When her and her uncle first moved out from back east, Dad always, my dad was a sympathetic guy.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He always felt for his brothers. He always helped all his brothers, more or less. And so he felt sorry for them and he hired her to cook one spring over there on the farm. And I guess he had a little work for her husband, too, on the farm. And then to top it all, later on, he got the both of them a job at a mill on Russell Ridge. Ramey Sawmill. Wasn't big money, but it was $60 or $65 a month, but they got bored. The two of them. And that's how they come to get a little money to buy this 40-acre tract out by duty. They're going to give $400 for it, see. Had a little log cabin on it. And that's where they were living when uncle got killed. Him and Uncle Gilbert was out in the woods sawing and I could tell you about how that happened. It was in the deep snow, see. And he tried to get, they saw this tree, but they hadn't side cut it. Now there's a trick that you've got to know something about when you're falling timber. If a tree's a-leaning, you better side that cut. If it's leaning heavy, especially.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I got so, I was pretty good at it. I cut wood up at Orofino. I mean, made a living cutting wood after I was married. Single-handed by no one thought, see. So, I fell in a tree, I'll tell you, show you now. There was a great big, I wouldn't have had to fell, but I just kind of got curious. Bosses said, well, you don't have to take that yellow pine, but if you want to, you can. Well, this tree I knew damn well I could fall it, because the son of a bitch was just putting air down in the way, leaning, see. Well, that's what I knew better than to try to cut behind. I cut both sides. I just kept a-cutting both sides, see, way in. Clear over to my undercut. You didn't have to have much undercut. Then I started in over here, and you know what that damn tree broke? About that much on the stump. Broke it, because it was leaning so heavy, see. Now, if that, here's what I wanted to illustrate to you. If I'd have done like my uncle and them, they didn't side cut, and that tree split up.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: See what I mean? Jumped up in the air, because it was on this, it was still fastened to the stump, but she split off, and then she fell over sideways, and my uncle was out here running away from it, and caught him in the side of the head and mashed his head. Killed him deader than a mackerel. That's the way he died. So what happened was it fell sideways. It fell.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did it split in two?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And he would happen to be right in the way, you see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did it split in two or just fall sideways?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No! You know what I, here's the idea. Let's see now, I'll get you, I'll illustrate from this flashlight. Say that this is the stump, and your tree, if you hadn't got it side cut it, this part of it still stayed on head, say, well about, I don't know how much it was, but it was enough to hold the tree up to here, say at 12, 15 feet. And it accidentally then happened to flop over to the side my uncle was, and he was right square in the way and caught him in the head. Oh, terrible. Mashed him down. Well, just killed him dead right now. One thing about it, he didn't suffer, he just knocked him out.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he have any, did he get any kind of, did you get any kind of insurance?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, I don't think, I don't think the company, no, you see them days, the Potlatch was pretty smart that way, they had them jippin', you get so much a thousand for cuttin'. See, when they took strips, that's what I did when I was up in the woods there in 36th, I had, I was gonna tell you that, I had three partners, we come by, at first my cousin, Ervin Swenson, he'd come over, I was a little, was neat and warped, dang bad, and he'd come over and said, Helmer, we had sawed together, and he knew I was good on the saw. He says, I said, I lost my partner, he says, I'd like to have you come over and help me out while he gets over. And that was another cousin of mine, Helwood, from Edvin Helwood. But he got poisoned from using that saw and got it scattered around his belly, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Using what on the saw?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: What they call, well, it would be, them days, I guess they used coal oil or diesel, which was the cheaper. I think they did use diesel quite a bit.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He got infected?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, no, that's what gave him the poison on his, or they thought that, might have been poison oak, I don't know. But anyway, he had to quit. Well, so, I went over there and went to work with Ervin. Well, as soon as he got, no, he didn't get him, he got another phone in my hair mailed for a partner. Well, then, I got toughened in, I worked, I think it was about two weeks then with Ervin, so I was pretty well toughened in, and they were shorthanded, 1936. And the boss come around at me and asked me if I'd be, want to go swamping. Well, I knew how to swamp, you know, cut the brush for temperature to go in the woods. Yeah, you bet, I said I would. $2 .75 a day. About $3 a day for board. So then, anyway, I worked that wood for quite a while, and I guess a couple of weeks and I'd swamp for several different guys.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: So, and I could buck a log. Now, you think, if a log is laying on Ervin, we'll say, up high, you start cutting that thing on top, it'll pinch your saw. Well, you can saw down maybe a half a saw depth to keep it from splitting your, ruining your log. Then you got to start cutting underneath. Well, I was wise to that, I just chopped the double-bitted X into the log I was sawing, and I put the back of my saw on that, and go at it this way. And I was stout, then I was primed, you know, I was only 36, wait a minute, wait a minute, wait a minute, I got to 36. Well, you was 48. No, hella, I was 48. Yeah. But I was husky, I worked hard all my life, and I was tough men, man, you see on this other work I'd done before I got there, so I could take it. So you... I was bad good, and so I was getting wind, pretty soon saw boys come around, you see, I was good on the saw, they figured I'd be pretty good to let it strip.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, they'd have a saw gang, they'd lay out a strip for each saw gang, see what I mean?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Maybe 40 acres, they'd blaze it out, and that's your strip, and your partner's strip. ... Yeah, gyppoed, sure. That's why I say that the company don't have to ensure when they're gyppoed. So he'd come around and... Yeah, so this saw boss, you big old tall fella, said, how would you like to have a partner and a strip? Well, I said, that'd be fine if I could get a good partner. If you don't get a good partner, it's a hell, you know, because if they ride the saw, well, you just can't make nothing. Yeah, he said, I think I got a good one, he says, from Bovill. Young fella, he was only 25, when I was 48, see. Well, I said, bring him out. I said, I'll try it, and by God, he was good. We neither one said a word. We sawed together, I guess, for a couple of trees, and pretty soon, I don't remember which one said first, you're just right up my alley, you know, we just got along fine. But we sawed together, and he'd give out, or that is his back, give out.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He said, come and apologize that he couldn't take it anymore, it was his back. He got his back hurt, I don't know, it was a year or so before that, and he said, that come back on him, he said, he just couldn't hack it. Well, God, I said, I'm sorry, I said, I would like to have you like that. So, well, then we got into some dry rot stuff, and I told the saw boss, God, we'll never make it in that, I said, that punk, you know, it rots up quite a ways, and you got to cut that off, that's counted. So, there's some saw in there that you lose. I said, that's all right, he said, you guys go ahead, it's got to be cut. He said, we'll make it right. I said, fine, took his word, you know. Well, then he gave out, then there was three North Carolina guys sawing in the woods, and they couldn't fall, they'd never been in the woods, they didn't know sick of them, nobody told them nothing of them, no wonder they didn't get hurt. They'd hang their trees up. You know, you get in there where there's a thick bunch of timber, you got to start, kind of figure out where the hell to start and keep falling.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And they didn't do that, and they just, they fought, I seen them one day, there's God, they worked a half a day, all three of them, and they didn't get the tree down. I don't remember what they done in the long run, we was too busy, we just left, we were busy cutting. So, anyway though, this one, name was Bob Hughes. He found out that I'd lost my partner, and he wanted to get on with somebody that knew how to handle the timber, see. So, he come over to me, and, no, the boss did first, saw me. She says, I've got a partner, and I said, who is it? When he told me, I didn't know how to believe it, you know. Well, he says, I'll send him in, and I said, okay. Well, he was good enough, he was a likable guy, he was just other than her, but he had a way about him that I couldn't help but kind of like him.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: So, I said, well, I'll try you out, buddy. I said, boy, I'll tell you now, you and your partners have sure had a hell of a time with it. You'll have to listen to me now, if we go to fall. I said, I want the whole say about it, how the fall is triggered. Sure, he said, that's what I want, he said, I don't know a damn thing. So, I thought, my God, that's all right then. Well, we saw on the way, saw on the way. He was a little bit slow to start with. Of course, I realized he wasn't used to it, and I just gave him time to get used to it. I thought, my God, I'm going to try and get along with him. I wanted to work. It was hard times, but, God, I had all them kids to feed. So, I guess the boy, let's see, that was 1936. Oh, my God, I think he was at home yet. Well, anyway, I went, we just saw on the way, and there was one tree that was hung up. We never fell it, I guess it was kind of a windfall hanging in other trees, and we had to cut that stuff.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And I said, Bob, when we fall this tree, if I have luck, I'll say, I don't want to hit that tree so it'll come out of there, and it's got to hit it 12 or 15 feet from the other tree, so it'll, I think that'll just about, something like that anyway, to loosen it out of there. But I said, when we do, if we have luck, and that tree gets loose, it's going to come down here just like a bullet, because there's steep mountains. And I said, Bob, I said, you go over there behind that green tree, and I said, I'll take care of the soil, so I'll go over this way, if I got time to take this off, if I ain't, I don't care. And by God, there happened to be a little sapling, six or eight inch cedar sapling, sitting pretty close to where he stood, you know. The damn fool ran behind that, and when this tree come and luck had had it, it didn't happen to hit him, but it hit this little tree, I polluted it, and that stumped when it broke up, see, stopped the damn tree. But he was down at the other end of this sapling that was coming down, and it caught him right on top of the head, and mashed him between his legs, and all I seen was the whites of the eye, and God, I thought, I thought maybe it half stunned him, you know.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And I didn't say a word till he got up and shook his head, and, and I said, shall you hurt Bob? Oh my God, but next time he tell me where to go, he said, I'm going back. Boy, I said, Bob, I said, if you're that tough, and I want to get in a fight with you, I couldn't knock you out, the tree can't knock you out, and I had a joke with you, you see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh now, now that tree come down?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, no, this was that little tree. The little one, yeah. Yeah, but it was only the top of it, and it would give, don't you see what I mean, but it was just enough, and him turned, he happened to turn around, and he stood there, you see, he had a foul, the tree got him fouled. He was, had his back down the hill, and the tree just happened to hold him enough that he didn't fall over, it just pushed him down, gradually. It didn't hurt him, no, he wasn't hurt a bit. He was just far enough to the end of that dog gone pink that it'd give enough, that it didn't, you know, knock him out. But it sure put life into him. Jesus Christ, he'd become a good partner after that. And boy, it had speeded him up. It did. Oh Christ, he just right up on his toes, God damn, he found out that it wasn't all just bullshit.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: You had, you're gonna get some, by God, you had to move. You're gonna make, see, we was only getting $1 .35 a thousand, you see, and you had to average $10 ,000 to get your bonus.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Ten thousand a day?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Ten thousand a day. You had to sell that much every day in order to, you got to average that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Then the bonus was at the end?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, that was added then, then you get that, but by golly, here's what I'm gonna tell you then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How much of a bonus was that, by the way, if you got it?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, a dollar a thousand. Okay. No, no, it wasn't that much, no, no, that's too much. It was $1 .35 a thousand to begin with, and I forget what the hell the bonus was now, but it's a certain amount. Okay, well forget it. Yeah, I can't remember that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So, what were you gonna say?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That's so long ago, see. Anyway, we got our book, well, I did, I mean, I went to that trip, as I say. Here then comes my brother, this diner that's in Parkland. He was working at, I was working for Axel Anderson, the foreman. Steiner was working for his brother, Malcher Anderson. And Steiner come crying over to me that he didn't like that filer over there. He said, I know you've got good filer over there, and he said, I'd just like to come and saw with you. Well, we had sawed together, you see, when we were cutting that wood on the ridge there on the homestead, so I knew he could saw, right? And so, God, I says, Steiner, I hate to turn this guy down, I just got him broke in, and it's too bad, I said, I hate to do that. Kind of a trick, kind of a dirty trick. But we were riding together back and forth to Park, and it was his car, too, I was riding him. So I had to kind of cater to him, see, a little bit. So I told Bob, I said, God damn it, I hate it, but I said, my brother's just up against it, I guess. I said, them filers over there is not much good. He give in, and he thanked me for learning him how, you know. So he got on again at some other work, I forget, probably another saw, but he worked in the camp.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Bosses didn't fire him because of that. Well, I think I told the saw boss that I had learned him, I said, he's a pretty good guy. I said, keep him on, I'd put him in any place now, I said, he's learned a hell of a lot from me. They kept him on. Oh yeah, I said, my brother and I, we finally, I was going to tell you, my brother, he took one day, he took another one, he's going to be the head faller. By God, it was crazy, I didn't mean, he did take them kind of streets, you know. And the tree was leaning, yeah, it was leaning downhill too much. You're supposed to fall uphill as much as you could to save the timber. It made it better for the loggers to hook on the butt end to log the drag, too. But you didn't have to do that all the time. If a tree was leaning to hell and gone and you had to work too hard to get it, they didn't expect you to.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And I told him so. Well, he just got a damn bullhead and he was going to have that tree fall in the way it should. I let him wedge, wedge, wedge trees in about half, three quarters of an hour and God damn, he was about all in. I said, Dina, I said, how about that? I said, let me spell you off. He said, get the hell out of here, all right. I said, he took him, see. I said, you son of a bitch, you're my brother, by God, you tough it out now. I let him go to it. He toughed it out and, well, he gave in then. I said, now, diner, I said, the next tree I'm going to fall it downhill regardless of where it leans. I'm going to show you to prove to you just what a little, little do. He was afraid he'd break it all to hell, see. So the next one I did, I fell it downhill. Then we got to one tree, no, two trees, growed together in the bottom.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Now that's a kind of a God damn puzzle, see. Which one to fall first? So I asked my brother, I said, no, I said, which one would you follow? He said, you see, you're following me, son. Well, I said, let's follow the upper hill first. We cut under there till we get our saws in enough to get the falling wedges in to hold it. And I said, we'll keep coming and let her go. After we got in, anyway, she even got the wedges in so as to get it off of the saw. You got to do that or there's some bitch you can't solve with them cross-cut saws. Or any saws, where's that go? So by God, yeah. He said, that'd be all right. And, well, I said, you see if it don't work. By God, it did that tree fell as putty as could be, see. Well, the down one doesn't have nothing to it. All we had to do was undercut and let her go.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: So from then on we got along pretty good. And I told him that time that he was arguing, I said, by God, I said, we got to cut out this arguing. I said, we got to just keep working. And he got pushed up and munged and I said, I don't have any time. He said, don't shut up. I said, I'm going to let you go to hell and I'm going to get a good partner or get another partner. And I said, I want another God damn word out of you. Just like that, see. I told him, by God, he said it. And we made it. We got our bonus. I told him that. I said, by God, if we don't shut up, I said, we won't get that bonus out of that. That saw boss is watching us all the time, I'll bet you. I said, he's out here in the woods somewhere. I said, he can see what's going on. Don't think for a minute, he ain't got his eyes on us. Whether we're fighting or working.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And by God, you know, that fall, hell yeah, we got our bonus. Everything went all right then. Well, that's the kind of a deal I've had in my lifetime. Oh, I didn't tell you about that accident I'd come putting you having with my brother that died with cancer. Well, we were sawing her in the long. And after this undercut cutter went away, you know, well then here comes this walking boss. He says, I'll undercut for you young roosters, I guess he thought. Well, he was out there and cutting away, but he was pretty cute. He understood the game and they were smart enough to put us young greenhorns away from the main gangs up above us. So, they put us down here on a little bench like and he cut in a circle on this bunchy to get ahead of us. He was fast. He could undercut, he played the game right. He'd get in there and chop out several trees instead of running along with one tree at a time, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And so while he was down here marking this tree, we were sawing on, we were sawing reaching up high like this. And then there was a bunch of logs laying over there that we had fell that were laying crossways at each other. Well, this wind come up and I heard the guys above us, timber down the hill, look down the hill. I looked up and there this damn tree looked like it was half way down, right at us. See the wind come up and blowed one down that was, this fella had got the good side and left rotten side so wind could flop it. And the end of that tree, I mean that tree just come right between our saw handles. But I was just that quick, I said, Sam, get under them logs and I beat him over there. I jumped over that log before that tree hit that. Now it could have caught me, but I had to do it. It was the only place I had to go.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: It's coming towards you which way you gonna go. You gotta get up there, you're fine to get under. And these loggers up high, we'd all both got under there and they did, when it landed between the saw and the top of that was where this sawbod, our walking boss was down at the other end of this tree we were cutting on. See he was down there marking and trimming. No, they don't trim, it's just marking. And that hit him, the end of that hit him just like this other tree hit this other guy. And it made him mad, see. Turned around and started cussing, I started cussing him back. I said, by God, you've been up there following them trees or cutting the good part and I said it's one of them that failed, wasn't it? He thought we was up there following trees. Almost killed him. He got, he didn't kill him, but... No, you, you. Yeah, it could have. So I told him, I said...

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, he got mad too. He said, well, you guys can do your own undercutting. From then on we did, you see. What little time we did finish the job up till we got, till Simon got in, my brother Simon got into the cook house and I got down there to hook him at the landing, see. And, oh, that's the way I transferred around. And I've had all them kind of accidents. Hell, when I was a hauling grain from that farm when I was a kid, 17 years old for Dad, I had a ... animal that ... three times in, that was the different hills we had to go to get to the grade to go down to Peck. And I beat it with a chain. Them days we had a, what they call a state chain that we didn't have a buck chain harness. We had just a state chain and I'd get down on the hound's wagon and beat it, see. And I could make it pull. I did make it pull. I had awful good leaders. That's what helped me. And they'd just claw for dear life anytime I let them have the lines, you know. So I said to myself, boy, you are going to work, boy, golly, find them yourself. Well, everything, I got them up all them hills until we got to Peck, across the ferry boat.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, there was another hill just where you get the warehouse, on the north side of the Clearwater River. And if the son of a bee didn't start balking him back, right down off the grade towards the Clearwater River. Man, I wasn't, I bet you I wasn't 30 feet from the north side of that river in how God knows deep. And I was down on the hound of that wagon, I'd beaten that son of a gun. My leaders were throwing rocks all over me. They tried to hold it, see. They did hold. Well, they backed down over a rock about a foot high, but after I got this other bastard to pulling, they lifted it right up and I just kept beating her clear on until I got to the warehouse. And the warehouseman, they hollered and they said, my God, kid, you come pretty good going in Clearwater, didn't you? I said, I sure did, but I said, my God, I was going to stay with it as long as I could. We're going to make that son of a bitch pull.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: From then on, that animal pulled for me all right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How high above the river was it when it went down? How high over, above the river were you when that?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, about 30 feet. That's all that was left until I'd have been down on the back horsing and all. Just to show you what kind of a deal that river was, now, it's ferry boat you had to cross on, see. You know what a ferry boat is, and that's not powered by steam, it was powered by the stream. They got a cable cross here that holds it, see, and they angle it, so the stream pushes it. That's the way it goes cross. I didn't know that. Yeah, that's another little trick that I never forgot. Well, then one time there happened to be what they call a jerk line skinner that hauled grain from our ridges and different ridges. He'd been an old fazer. He had a big brownie, he called him, that was his jerk line leader. Then he had a fast horse alongside of him with a jockey stick that when he guided it, he'd throw the line on which side to this brownie that was trained in, see. That horse would have to go, he'd have a fast horse, he'd have a hold back trap so he'd only get so far ahead, but he had to stay so far away from brownie.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, everything went fine until one day he was home. Oh, God, he had big wagons. One of them, I guess the trail wagon itself was, they called it four inch. Now, three inch is a small wagon, but four inch, that's a heavy something. That was bigger than any one wagon we ever had, but he'd been a big freighter for you in rough country. And he said, if you got a big wagon, he said, no matter how much load you pull on it, he said, well, God, it'll pull easier than a little wagon. We didn't know that, but that's what he claimed. But here when he come on this fireboat one day, and he had a big team in the wheel, they weighed about, I guess, a ton of piece. And a swing team, he had six on, see. He was hauling a hundred sacks or better to a load. And God dang the minute he got on this here with all these outfit and the big wagons and all that load, that God damn boat had sprung a leak and down she went.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And the horses went head on into the river. But he was quick enough that he got his swing team and leaders back, the wheelers. See, by that time the wheelers was shoved in head first down there. He lost the wheel team. Yeah, I don't know whether he ever got any money out of it or not. I don't think so.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now, what did you have to do to break them off there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, you see, they have a, I don't know how he had it rigged, but generally the way I had it was you'd have a chain from either chain or rod. We used to have a rod back instead of a chain with maybe a hook to the lead boss. He'd jerk that hook out of there and then they'd be free. They'd come back, you see. And he had his, lucky he probably wouldn't have done that had he had his horse trained, that leader, that Brownie, you see. He was trained good. He didn't have to do much to him. He could just throw that line which way, come on Brownie or something like that, and boy that horse would ride around. He knew they were dangerous. He was a good sensible horse. He trained him good. And so he saved his swing team and Brownie and his partner. It went down that fast. You just put them on the boat and it just went down that fast. Yeah, when the boat started sinking, it was gone. So that's where it's been going and all. And then I got on after I got to farming on Centler Ridge. Now dad, I made pretty good with them hogs. I'd raised hogs for two years. First year, I didn't do so good.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I'd just done enough with one sow and she had, you see, nine pigs. And so I had her in a lot, but I think it's a quarter or half an acre, that I'd seeded down to oats, green oats and peas, combination for pasture, because we hadn't well felt by that time. Then I had a feeder there that I fed her barley, chopped, rolled barley. And by golly, in five months, them little devils growed to be around 200 pounds apiece. And that's what started me getting in hogs. And I took them to Orofino. There's no market in Peck. I had a hog cleared to Orofino, but I got 17 cents a pound. Well, that made me $34 a hog, see. Well, I got the figuring on that. I said, gee whiz, that's more money than I can raise, get off of raising wheat. So the next year, that's when I called on dad to get to move that house for a hog house. And I didn't finish telling you all that. Now all that, every 400 feet, we had to keep digging down three feet in hard pen to pull, to anchor, to pull that house, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I just had a coyote team pulling this stump puller, and every 400 feet you had to dig that. In that field I showed you up there, because I wanted to get up on top of that hill. I didn't want to go in the side hill or slide off my skids.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now you put it on skids?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I made them skids out of bull pine logs, peeled them so they'd be slick. And I and a neighbor jacked the house up and slid them under, and then we reinforced it here in front to hook to the pull by, see. And drug that three quarters of a mile through that field, and just as we got it into the hog lot where I was going to put it, or pretty near where I was going to put it, was on some orchard grass. The storm broke, and I was carried along in November, see, I was worried about the weather. I thought, my God, if I could get stuck in the field with that plowed ground, it'd be pretty messy. But I happened to make it. Didn't have to, didn't have, I mean I got in on that sod, orchard grass sod, just when it started bad weather. And I finally moved it over, I told my neighbor, I said, I can finish now, I said I'll move that over there myself. So I didn't have him no more, but I moved it over close to this pond, that's a pond laying there, close to them trees there. I moved it over there and I set it up on foundation high enough that I, three or four feet high, leveled it up, see, and had it high enough so my stock hogs could go underneath. And I could, I had, that was a big enough house that I could have, I had seven sows on one side of Piedgang Way, and seven on the other, fourteen brood sow. And I, they hatched, I took good care of them, I'd learned how to take care of a brood sow, see my brother and I, we took up, we went to the university here and got some agriculture training, two years.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that the short courses that you had?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That was the short course, yeah. It was six month courses, but it done us a lot of good, because we hadn't got, only we didn't get to eighth grade, until we got to go to Spokane College that Dad had took a share in, see, and they didn't charge anyone that bought share in it, wouldn't have to pay a tuition. All we had to pay was our board and room, and that was only four dollars, well there was two rooms, eight dollars a month, and then there's only two ninety a week for board.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: At Spokane. ... I'll have to ask you about that later. Yeah. Now tell me about them pigs and that.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, well anyway, I had awful good luck, that first year especially, I mean that's the second year. So I wrote, or I fed them carrots and alfalfa leaves, and boy them little alfalfa grew like everything. They was having Duroc jerseys, see that's a good, Red Hog, they're a hardy hog, and prolific. They had, I had, they averaged, well there's, like I said, I had them fourteen sows, brought me a hundred and nine pigs. And I saved a hundred and five out of that bunch. No kidding. And so, but I had to borrow money to buy, buy feed because I hadn't thrashed nothing for myself yet. I went to the bank, I said, Dode, he was, the bank had been broke too and the farmers had been, had organized the bank and they had took it over for, well you might say, they had to reorganize and run it. The tax bank, yeah okay.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And Dode Holmes was the president of it at that time. He was one, just a farmer like ourselves, up there on Central Ridge. And so I got to go see him to get by with this money.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What, about what year would this have been?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well that was in 19, let's see, wait a minute, about 1919. And, wait, no wait a minute, no.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Maybe a little later?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, later, wait a minute, it was 1923. Okay. The second year. Because the last year I quit, 24. Okay, so it was 23. It was 23, 1923. And by golly, when I told Dode, you know, well thank God, he says, I can't let you have it, he says, I've got to call up the directors and find out, he says, them directors, he says, have got more say really than I have. Well I said, Dode, I'll tell you one thing, I said, I don't want you to take my word. You come up and see my hogs so you know what you can tell them, not tell them what I said. And, so he did, he come up the next morning. And the little devils, it happened to be a nice sunshiney day, and I had a rant, see, the little devils was out here in the sun, sunning themselves, and they'd play around, they'd feel pretty good, see, they was about putting your weaning time, and these little roly poly devils, just fat as a roll of butter. And so when they could smell a stranger, they'd get scared, see, they'd woof woof woof woof woof. They just felled that whole god damn ramp, and the sunshine in the morning looked like gold nuggets flying up there.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: My god, Dode says, woo, he says, that beach, everything, he says, well, he said, you didn't tell no lie. Alright, Elmer, he says, I'll call the bankers, we had a phone them days, I'll call you if it's okay. So he says, the next morning it'll take probably a day or so to find out from the directors. Next morning or the other, a couple of days after that at least, I found out, he called me and said, come down and get your money. Well, I finished them hogs up with that borrowed money, because I didn't, I told Dode, I said, I'm gonna make a bin on the, Dad had this barn there, you see, and it was 50 foot wide, where that driveway is, and I made a bin all along on that side, and that held 1400 bushels. So that fall I just, I put the grain in the bin. I didn't sell a darn kernel, I was lucky I did, because the wheat that I had on the fall wheat got smutty, and I wouldn't have got four bits of bushel for the wheat, besides the sacks and the hauling and all, see, all that extra trouble. Of course there was trouble with feeding the hogs, but, that was another little sticker, Dad, he didn't want, first he didn't want to consent to sharing like he did with the grain, that was a third. He wanted half.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Half of the hogs. I didn't know that. I said, now you get a third of the grain, I ate two thirds, but I got to stand at all expenses. Yeah, but he said, you don't have as much expenses. No, but I said, I'll have more work. Well, but he said, you ain't got the sack bill, you ain't got the hauling bill, don't make any difference. I said, if we both make money, and I do all this extra work, I said, this is the only way I'll take it. He finally consented. So that's what it was. That way we don't have to keep track of the wheat. Put it in the bin and feed it. Divide the hogs. And by God, he finally consented. He finally, see this was after, I'd been there, uh, in 23. Yeah, I had, still had a lease, you see. Wait a minute, oh, I see, 23, 23, no. That was, my lease was out. I had got it for five years. And, uh, he's the one that coaxed me to stay two more years. I told him I was going to quit. I didn't have to then, my lease was out. And, uh, no, I said, you better stay. He said, well, I'd given him good rent plenty before that, see. Even off of the grain. Because he got a third clear.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: So, yeah, because I didn't tell you that, I'd raid the crop of beans on that particular spot where that flax is raved. I had 44, that was one crop I had that done pretty good. I got, uh, 1300 pounds an acre and, uh, Dad could have got as much money, I mean a third as much money as what I did. I sold mine for $2100, my two-thirds share. Off that crop of beans. And then the next year it was, that I got, uh, I was lucky on the wheat, I didn't get a big yield, we didn't fertilize like they do nowadays. We just, uh, and I was greenhorned at starting the farming. I didn't know how to do, like, I learned afterwards. And, and this, this ground of Dad was, had been in clover and it was loose. Instead of letting it stay loose, I should have packed it. And I only got, uh, well that Marcus wheat then was a poor year, 16 bushels.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What year?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, that was, that was about, uh, 1900 I think. Wait now, wait now. No, no, it's been later. Maybe 200, 21, something like that. Nineteen. That was the time when I was born. That's when I had the beans, 1918. Beans was 18, so this would have been 19. This was either 19 or 20. Oh, okay. And, uh, then I got the, and I, I, I was hauling that wheat at Marcus, see. The guy at warehouse money, I was hauling that to this side, that didn't cross the river on that side, that was after they got two, two warehouses, one on each side of the river. And I didn't want to fool around and go across. Sometimes you, them other guys would get ahead of you and you had to sit there and wait, see. And they paid practically as much, not quite as much as the other side, but you didn't have to cross that damn ferryboat.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: So I sold to Crawford. So, uh, on this side. So you got only a poor yield. You only got 16 bushels of acre. Well, I did, but what I was going to say, I got a big price, see. When I was hauling, I had, I had kept the ground clean because I had plowed my ground in the fall, and then I would disk it in the spring in the harrowed. First I harrowed it to get the fowl stuff going. So it made it awful.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did it get the what stuff growing?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Wild oats and ... wheat and stuff like that. So when I got two of that, uh, that way, it made a nice clean wheat. And this market was good, the flower wheat made good flower, see. And Crawford was interested. He said, uh, how much of that you got? Well, I said, I got a, counting my dad's share, I said, I got a thousand and nineteen sacks. Ninety, I forgot which it was now. And he said, uh, well, I said, uh, what do you take for it? Well, wheat had been going two twelve, two fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, and back down to two ten twelve. So, you jumping around like that. Pretty soon when he struck me, he says, how would you like two twenty? He says, by God, you know, I says, that's all right. I says, I'll take that or you can give me more if you want to. So, well, he said, that's, that's top price. When you get it all down, he says, you haul it all down. He says, we'll settle for that. I says, okay. So, next day I come down.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Say, he says, how would you like two twenty five? He says, I understand the other warehouses are paying more than I offered yet. I said, I don't want to be as good as they are. Well, hell, I said, you can make it two and a half, you want it. So, I got two and a quarter. See, that's how the price, I mean, that crop yielded pretty good. Sure. In money. Five thousand one hundred dollars. Dad got seventeen hundred dollars cash. Besides, I had to pay him three hundred dollars for seed wheat and the hay that I had to feed my outfit for the next year. So, that's why he was doing pretty good, don't you see?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And, what about that, that, that was this farm here. Peck, Idaho. Central Ridge. I'm thinking now that the pigs, you didn't really finish telling me what happened with them pigs. Well, that fall, yeah, when I paid, when I, that fall when I sold them, by golly, I didn't get a big price for the hogs. Now, that first fall, that first fall I only got six, six and a half cents.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Two hundred pound, only thirteen dollars for thirteen, I mean, for a two hundred pound hog. See, it wasn't one half what I got at Orr Field that time. So, shipped them to Spokane, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, did you sell the whole, whole, whole, bunch?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, I sold them for that, but, and that only made me, well, let's see now, I got thirteen dollars, and, well, I made enough, so I, I, I had a little money left to make, pay my expenses and live on them, and I paid the bank up the five hundred dollars, see. I had to pay the bank the five hundred dollars. And, so the next year then, what I was going to say, next year I had all kinds of experience, man on man. Talk about tough times. My wife got sick of that, see, she brought birth to a dead boy, baby boy, weighed over ten times, ten pounds, see, she went over time. She had what they called, at that time, they called it Bright Disease, I don't know, maybe she had diabetes then. And, this doctor that come and took the baby away from her, she put in her past, she passed out. And, God, there I was left for them three little kids, Jesus scared the devil out of me. There was three older ones, that's the two girls and the boy, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And, he was only, oh, see, that was, what year did I say that? It was 19, yeah, that was 1924. And, well now, let's see, the boy would be, he would be six and the other girl would be four. Oh, wait a minute, I got ahead of myself. The boy was eight and the other girl was six and four, youngest girl was four. They were just kids. And, but she finally come to, see, God, I was relieved. I sure held my breath for a while, till she come to.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long was she out there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, she was down, God, that's when I say. That spring I had to tend to them kids, do my own cooking, tend to my horses and some cattle ahead and hogs, sows. God, I got up at three o'clock in the morning, I had to get up that early to get my work done, get out in the field to do a day's work. Go to bed at nine, ten, eleven o'clock at night. It's all the sleep I'm getting. But I got that fall, I was just a skeleton, believe it or not. And not only that, I had two mares a-folding and I had this ground that was west of the barn there towards my uncle's place. I had that in the summer fall of that year and had it in the corn and peas that I wanted to fatten these hogs on, see. I did that over that other summer fall or two and I didn't tell you that, I had corn on it. I found out that it was the slickest way, half of it in the corn, half in the peas and they would eat the peas first and then by that time the corn would be ready and then they'd go right into the corn, see. And Dad had his place fenced hog tight. And I was the instigator that talked him in the notion of fencing that hog place hog tight. And he never raised a hog, I mean to make any money, till I got on it.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That's why he wanted to keep me there, he thought Jesus Christ, I really don't want to tell you though. And after twenty-four then, when the price come up, I was in debt, forty-four hundred dollars.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Which year, the year that your wife was sick?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, I was in debt, forty-four hundred dollars and I told her, I said, well Dad, I was having trouble with a neighbor there, his kids had been picking on my boy and I wanted to get the hell out of there. And I said to Dad, I said I want to quit. I said I'll sell out everything to you, I said for what I owe you, I'll sell out everything to you. I allowed him two thousand dollars for somebody down here, for his outfit at first and that was what I went into debt for. Allowed him two thousand, see. Well, and then equipment and that is for everything. I went in debt to him, listen, and then I still owed him eleven hundred and sixty dollars. And I wanted to wipe the slate clean if he'd take my outfit, including two colts and two extra horses, oh, see with him. No, it was two colts and the five horses I bought of him, see I had seven, I was farming with seven heads. Five heads that I bought of him and a brand, not a new binder, but an eight foot binder and another drill, his drill and binder wasn't to suit me.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And a chop mill cost a hundred dollars and no, he couldn't see it. I knew I'd have a problem, you know, dealing with him. Well, I said Dad, I'll tell you what I'll do, he wanted me to sell out. But first he said, why don't you stay? No, I said Dad, I'm going, I said I've got the hunch to go and I said, why don't I go? Because I worked like a damn slave all summer and I said I ain't going to take it no more. He said, by God, I want to get out of here. I said, no, I'm in deep debt, and I said, by selling the hogs now? That's what I didn't tell you. The hogs went up, you see you had to sell half of them before you did the other half because that's the way they fattened out. And I got eight and a half cents for them and the other's ten and a half and the wheat jumped up to a dollar forty-five or fifty. I said, by doing all the selling now, I'll clean you and the bank and I'll have a little to live on.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And I'll have a team, oh yes, there's another thing I forgot to tell you. The bank is, God damn that's what raised hell with me. It got us interested in some of these Guernsey cows. We bought Guernsey in there and I had four heads to move with. That is two heifer calves and two cows to move to park with. And I figured I could go over there and there was plenty of pasture and go into cattle and raise a little hay, see. Take it more easy and go out to work in between. Which I did, but what I couldn't say, the old man he resented, oh he didn't want to take it. But I said, finally I said, listen, you mark down everything you've paid for the so and so horse and I said I'll mark it. I wanted to put it on two sheets so there wouldn't be no misunderstanding because he tried to jume out of it, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Which we did. And he shook his head and hell it come to fourteen hundred dollars right ahead of him. He had put his own price on. I told him eleven hundred sixty what I would do, I wanted this square with him. But when we got two figured up, it come to fourteen hundred dollars. His own price and he sat and he didn't allow me near what the horse, I said God you ain't paying more than about half what them horses cost me. Yeah but they're older, well alright I said. Well your sheet, you made up your own sheet and you had a working horse. And the same, we both marked what he agreed to pay. I see. And when he sold out, wait now. So help me, he had kids to help him for him see. And he had a damn kid cuddin' and some other kids, hoe and beans I guess. God damn they were sleeping up in that barn and burnt the god damn barn down, burnt his hay and harness and every god damn thing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did he do that?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well the kids was up there sleeping and they struck a match to try to find some candy mind you, the damn little brats. So then that broke his heart right so he wanted to quit himself then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's when, that was after you?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh that was after I moved out, yeah. You see we squared up.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh square up now, did he take your outfit then?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh yeah he took that. He knew he was getting a good deal then. There but then when he sold, I don't know if I can tell you there. When he sold out I told him, I said Dad you can always sell for better money than I can. Because he had been an insurance agent in that country, clear up around this place. I said you got a lot of old timers that'll come and bid good on your safe. Being that you've had this hard luck. Which they did. By God people come from all over, up around where he'd been canvassing, selling this fire. He started that farmers mutual fire insurance company and they all flocked in there and God they just gobbled up his stuff like nothing. And paid big price, he got double what I got for it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well this is because did he go around and tell them he was going to have the sale?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No they could phone around them basically. Or they had newspaper, I don't know how he did it. But they all come because he was well known in the country. Oh yeah because he had old friends everywhere. They felt bad about the fire. Yeah and they felt bad for him for that fire. Well I did buy, just to show you, I did, he had a little old bottle of tea, car. Tury. 19, what was that? Oh about a 19, 12, 15 something like that. I bought that in 55 dollars. It's the only thing I bought of him. Of course I had to pay him later, I didn't want to dig up, maybe he took it out of what I had coming. You see I had some coming.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How many years after you sold him did this happen? Was this many years later?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No it wasn't too many. Let's see, I guess that would be about, right now, 26, 27. No yeah here I'm getting a little far ahead. After the year or two years, 24, 25, 25 I worked out in the farming country here hauling grain. I bought a, made a down payment on a Model T truck, ton truck. So I went out and picked up sacks after a combine. She made a little money that way. But I lost it because I couldn't make the payments and I just let them take it. So after that I just went out and sown sacks in the harvest. But anyway. What I want to know is that before we get ahead of yourself, you're saying that I want to know about the year that you sold out to your... Well that's 24. That was 24. And I think he, then the 26 and 27 was the wet years. See I would have got sunk. He lost grain. That's what made him quit. He didn't want to lose his barn.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: But he lost grain. The wet years rotted the shocks. I worked on combines down here by Pullman. By God when it was damn wet, we worked 21 days and it started raining. Got some muddy, see. And the wheat got so soft. And so anyway, he finally quit then and he sold, he gave his place away. He finally sold that place for $10 ,000. The guy that bought it had a pretty good back and he had a half a... Yeah he had a half a... No. He had a quarter section of land before that. But he was in the clear and he had some folks, I guess his mother had a little money and they had enough to start buying it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well in 24 when you quit, did you get out of debt entirely when you sold it?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That's when I'm going to tell you how hard up I got. I come over here to park and dad was, he resented me enough. He owned that granddad place but he wouldn't let me rent there, I mean live there. But I played smart. I had cash rent, cash money so I went and rented a fellow by the name of Corn Place. For $100 a year, the whole place, that's all I paid him. And I moved my cattle in there and they had a good barn there, good log barn, good house, just as good as dad's on the homestead. Now wait, now before you tell me this, now you're saying the cattle, you had said before... Well I got these cattle.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, now did them cattle put you in debt?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: They sure did, I kept staying there, I was going to tell you that. I kept staying there, see, too long. I come there in 24. And I stayed on this corn place till 28 and I got sick and tired of paying that $100 a month, or a year. Because boy it was, well here, the cream prices went down so low. You know what it got so that I could only get a dollar and a half for a five gallon can of cream? And usually I couldn't raise enough hay on that little shirttail farm to feed them. So there was a doctor in there, had 90 acres of good land, pretty level land, that I rented for to cut... What they call bull pine trees for the rent. So I'd get the whole crop myself. It was a, and the only thing, they didn't have cattle water there, only a certain time of the year. And when it got dry summer I'd either haul water or drive them three miles to a pond. I got so I had to haul with a tank for our, yeah for wash water. There wasn't drinking water down in the draw there.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Now this other place had a good spring on it, see, but, and it really was the place, but it just didn't have ground enough.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It had a, it was a hundred dollars, a hundred dollars, was that it?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, a hundred dollars a year for the whole place, I'd get what I could raise on it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you were getting worse and worse off this time when it went on there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, I stayed there, you see, in part, on this doctor's place from 28 to 32. And I had a hell of a bunch of cattle. I'd been, well, one year I bought some state land, see, that was for dad, I mean before I rented over there, and dad, he didn't think I'd done a wise trick, which I didn't, but I didn't know it. I wanted some land, and there was 80 acres laying up and down alongside of one of these places that I rented, and it was state land. And I bought that for, see, 10 % down, $1400 for the 240's. And I had to pay down $400 cash, see, I borrowed that from my brother Simon, that's, died when he was 64. I paid him back though, and, yeah, I paid him back when I was farming over there, he was paid back when I was farming on the big place. But anyway, I stayed there on that place, and I tried to log that place, and could have got it logged if it hadn't, if snow hadn't have melted, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I bought a team, heavy team, and went in debt on that, and I bought a wagon, team and wagon, and a bump sled, and heavier harness, and I had to borrow $1000 in the Deary bank to do this… so then,… the snow, the snow left, you see, and I couldn't, I got a soil man to help me soil this big tree, big nice tree on Dr. Spree. He had consented to me at logging it, and he would have got his share out of that, to only just pay me for logging it, see.
