And I would log my own, that is that state land, I had a few thousand on it, so I'd pay it. No snow, this one, no snow next window, no snow, no snow, I'd just give it up. Well then I stayed there from 28 to 32, and the price of weird loats and everything went down, down, down. And Cal, you couldn't give that bunch of Deary stuff away, I really was broke that time. If I hadn't had them god damn things, I could have been working out, and done a lot better, and I told the mister, for god's sake, let's quit.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I says, the bank, I hate to quit, but I says, the bankers loaned me that money, I still own the $1000, but I says, well, they got the mortgage on the cattle, I says, I'll just let them take them for the $1000. Now if it had been prices like what I give, $125 for one of them cows, when I bought. And then I couldn't sell them at all. That's how bad the times were. Now some of these times, some of these kids around think, by god, they're having a tough time now. By god, they ought to have had what I had. And they'd think different. Oh, I got to tell you a little incident about it, a little accident I should say. My uncle, Ed Swenson, was with me, he'd been in the park there, he used to come in there, he lived at Deary then. He used to come in there and do a little hunting, and him and his brother Adolph and I. So I was taking these cream cans out to Deary in a bobsled, and I also had a buggy in there, because when I got to the highway, I had to take that buggy out and drive on the highway four miles.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I had this Cayuse team with a couple of brown gildings on there, and we got up the hill going, we had two cans of cream in there like I said. And it wasn't much, I didn't get much out of them, but well that time I think they were about $3 a can maybe, a $5 can. Well, God damn this one wild Montana cow he said I had, he got a bit out of his mouth. And he got scared when he could see back, and he started to gallop and run away. And I got scared, he got me shit up my neck, I jumped out the back of the sled with a hay rack on it, I said, Ed, I said, get out of there, let them go! You get hurt! I said, you get hurt, you know, you're stumped on the side of the road, crazy horse is running away, let them go! And I said, for God's sake, no, he stayed and held them. God damn, he stayed right with them, it was just luck and havoc. There were some woodcutters in the road, damn pretty, by that time the horses had just about threw runs in there, it was all winded, see, and they come out in the road, they see there's a runaway, they stopped them! And I had to walk about a mile, a mile and a half to catch up.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That spilt the cream, didn't have it wired on, they fell down, and maybe, oh, enough for a little coffee or something. See, Ed was busy holding the horses, the cream ran out while he was having trouble. Well, we got to Deary, er, to Helmer then, and loaded the buggy out, and I guess we must have took, took it all in. Well, Ed had to go home, I think that's the way it was, I took him in, you see, he wanted to get home. And, er, well then another time, when I was, that, I'll tell you that story too, that's a true, it's all true stories. So then, er, that's when I was living on this doctor's place, selling this cream. In the summertime, we had a neighbor that we always exchanged work with, wrists. And they had a pick-up, and I didn't, and I was, like I said, I was working out in the harvest field a lot of times, and we made the agreement that if she would haul, she was the one that drove it, if she would haul my cream in the summer, I would haul her cream in the winter. So, er, she would take that pick-up, see, and haul her cream when I was out to work. That way it got, got to market. Well then, by golly, wait now, yeah, one winner there, it's no, God, it's no, that's too, poor feature.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And boy, you couldn't go, one team couldn't go through that with any kind of a load of talk. Well I, lucky enough, I had a friend, this poor guy now, he just died here last week, Charlie, Charlie Jelliberg, I talked to him. Charlie Jelliberg, he had a team, and, er, Earl Austin had a team, and I had four, we put eight horses on, and I made a double, I mean a collapsible snow plow out of planks. I just got that idea and figured that we, we could snow plow, we got to the bottom of Potlatch, and then when we get there we just take them out and it'd just be the empty planks for the horses to pull back, because they'd be tired. By God, the boys, they agreed. And but hell, the other side wasn't plowed nothing. Next morning I had to take that seventeen cans of cream out to Deary with that Cayuse team and that snow to foot or two that night.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I had to break that road down to Potlatch that much, and then I had to go up and break my own road, and I would go dressed the way to the highway with that one Cayuse team, I'd take the doubletrees off, see. I learnt that when I was working for Doc Palmer at Potlatch, he told me in that deep snow I had to just break a road with a team and a doubletree. And that was off to the haystack, see, off the main road.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mean you broke the road just by using the doubletrees?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, well, enough so the horses could get through. Doing that snow season, yeah, I remember that. You broke that, now when you did that, explain to me again how you did that. You used a doubletree and the horses just enough to... Yeah, I went up the hill, see. Two or three times you had to go with that deep snow, don't you see… pack it down… and then I'd pull them a load, fourteen cans of cream, as far as they could go, and puff them, and go a little ways and puff them, and then when I'd get to as far as I broke the road, then I'd have to unhook again and go on. Well, what I was going to say, it took me from six o'clock in the morning to get to Helmer. I had to stay at Helmer all night. You know where the Helmer is. An old Carl Lancaster, his dad-in-law had a Wilkins. Wilkins, sure. Yeah, they had a barn, log barn. I asked them if I could stay all night or so, I'll pay for it. Well, that's all right, they said, and he had a store there, too, see, and he said they had hay.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I had my own grain, and next morning, you know, I wanted to pay, and they wouldn't even take us in. There's a good friend of mine, that's Carl, the Rancaster. We'd meet each other and have good old time talks once in a while, you know. I know him. I like him a lot.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you say puff them, what do you mean puff, puff them?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, that means resting them. Yeah. Did that go in there? What? That's my talk now?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, yeah, yeah. I'll take that. Hey, now listen, don't let it stop you from talking. I'm just the same as we were talking before. Well, that's the way it went, and let's see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: You know, it's like I said, I got there, it took me twelve hours, six o'clock until six o'clock.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about getting back? Was that okay then?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, I finally, the next day, Uncle Ed lived in Deary then, and so I made it a point to go there the next day with my team and buggy. See, I had the buggy then there, already there. And so, you see, I parked it there at Wilkins's from the time before. And so then I stayed all day the next day with Uncle to rest my horses. My God, they'd had a hard day of it the day before, see. I wasn't about to kill them entirely. They done awful good to plow that road. There was about two miles that I broke all by myself… you see… uphill business put near me. Well, not quite, but there's a lot of it anyway. That grade, you know how long that is. Well, that wasn't this grade, that was the old grade. It was worse than this one. Yeah, that was the old grade, so that was quite a bit different. That was the other, that was across the road. That was before the Potlatch got the road in there, you see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And, anyway, I got through it and so I just rested. The next, I guess I won't tell that, maybe it's a doll. It's one neighbor that never used to haul, exchange, hauling cream. And he called up Ed Swenson to see how I made it. And, of course, I liked the monkey. I told him, fine. I said, it's good now. I said, get to get him to come out, see. And he come out the next day and it took him till two o'clock to get to Deary. And I met him on the street and he says, I thought you said it was a good road. Well, I said, I figured it was a lot better than when I went. I had to break it all by myself. I said, you ought to be ashamed of yourself, as if being an old timer in there. You wouldn't even as much as offer to haul my cream can, let alone any other combination. And I said, boy golly, I said, the wrist always did.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I said, there was a real neighbor. We neighbored back and forth like neighbors should. And, well, he said, it sure took a long time to get through there. Well, I said, that's good for you.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you say two o'clock, you mean two in the morning?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, he was lucky to get there. He had a good fresh tea, of course. And my horses and the sled had broke a road. It hadn't snowed anymore. He could get through it pretty good. He might have to rest his horse a little bit when going up the grade. But other than that, he could plug along. He couldn't go fast, but he could.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So, when he got in there at two in the afternoon, what time would you get in there if things were just smooth? If things were smooth, what time would you get in there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, I could make that and bought, well, general rule... Let's see. I'd go over, let's see, about, oh, not over two hours… whew! Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, you tell me, just how important was that neighboring? Huh?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How important was that neighboring when you were in Park? Did people neighbor really close?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, the thing was, us folks at grade had cream to sell, see the idea. Especially when I went out to work in the harvest field. Then it was very important for me to see that my cream got out. My wife couldn't drive. She had little kids to take care of in the garden. So, with Mrs. Ritz, she was a nice neighbor lady there… she lived close by there. She'd always drive in, pick up our cans, take them out. Well, that's the way that went, oh, I tell you. Well, then, now here's some more if you want to hear the rest of it. ... Well,… in 1932, as I said, I told the bank, I made the agreement with the bank that they was to take my outfit for the mortgage. And I was going to have a clean slate. And I got into it, my dad and my uncle, Ado, was helping me to move out. I had a little what little I could haul out on this car. No, it was a Ford truck, that's right, a tongue truck. And I got down, oh, I didn't tell you, I made an arrangement with Angelie, lived out here southeast of Moscow, to live on his place for the rent, do his chores for the rent, so I could get my kids to school.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And so then, of course, when we got down to Troy with my load coming in to get over to this place, this Angelie had put in, yeah, I'd already unloaded one load. But I didn't tell you that I'd brought one load first, some fruit and stuff. And I come in, well, here he had another family in there. Man, was I mad. And Dad says, oh, you better turn back. No, Dad, I says, I'm going, so I'll make that devil cough up. And I was awful mad because of that. And anyway, I told him, I said, Uncle, I said, well, let's go into Moscow and see if we can find him. So we found out he was in the pastime in Moscow there. Well, I says, Adolph, call him out. I says, I can't go in there, I'd fight him right in there. I said, you better call him out. All right, he called him out, didn't he come out there. And I said, you done me one dirty trick, I said. Promised me that place to do the chores, and I said, you moved another family. And after I had possession, if I'd been smart, I could have sued him, you know. I was smart enough to do it. Dad didn't think of it.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: We could have had one, but I didn't want to be in that kind of a pickle, don't you see? I had a family there moving. I had to get someplace. So, well, I said, it's going to cost you plenty, buddy. We're going to stay right here until you fix up something. Well, he was pretty slick. He found this neighbor, friend of his, I should say, mix, GovMix. He says, I'll call him up, see if I can, he got a house back in the backfield. He said, he might let you have and get some work from him. Fine, I said, good, well. Oh, yeah, and he had offered me $25, you know, for damages, but I found out afterwards, when he got me that, I was big-hearted and give it back to him. And I found out I wouldn't have got that cashed anyway, because his credit was no good… there's checks… so I got a, I moved the family out there to mix this place, about three miles out in the country, in the dirt road.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And my kids, these older girls, they were, let's see, how old was they then? Twenty, thirty-two, wait a minute, thirty-two. This youngest one, she was seven, you see, she was born in twenty-five. And eighteen, see, the oldest one was fourteen, I guess. You know, eighteen, twelve, yeah. And the other one would be twelve, twelve, fourteen, and five. And the boy, he would be sixteen. Anyway, they had to walk to school all that distance, in that dirt road. Stormy old... And I had to get up and milk cows for that bugger, five o'clock in the morning, and then fix fence during the day. Little old dollar a day. Bored myself, built my family on that dollar. Well, he wasn't going to charge me no rent, to start with, until I got it. Them days, that was the year that old Roosevelt had the WPA. And it was a rock crusher, and Moscow wasn't all rock streets. Down here on Lewis Street, they had to have four horses on a wagon, just a little bunch of rock in the bed of the wagon would sink down halfway. It happened to be, what year, see, thirty-four that year that I got that job. And it was running down, I mean the wagon would sink down halfway on the spokes.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And I was out there pounding with a sixteen pound ball, what they call a nigger head, to get them through the rock crusher. And, forty dollars a month, that's all you got. But you wasn't starving on it, you could get by. And I got this house rented after I quit that son of a gun. See, I got a house on Polk Street for ten dollars a month. And they'd had a big fireplace in the basement.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So, you said he didn't charge you at first, then he didn't charge you at the end.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, yeah, and then when I quit, I had money coming from him, but he held that out for rent. He charged me seven dollars and a half a month rent. So it absorbed all I had coming, see, all he was just slicker. So I got stung that way anyway, but I made it. I got over to, got moved into, oh yeah, here was the deal. His pal was a McLean, he was a bookkeeper there in this place, see. And, so he wouldn't put me on right away, but one day after I got moved, yeah, he said, you're farming out there, you're on a farm. So I'm not farming, I'm just living there, working for Micks. They couldn't put me on, he said, on that account. Now they were cronies, see. But old Harvey Smith, he was a civil engineer, he was a boss of the whole works. And I come in there one day and I was telling them about this house that I had rented right here in town. I had moved in town and I wanted to get on. No excuse, I couldn't after I got in town. Because out there we had to haul water even. No water, there was a well that was there, was dead rabbits in it. Couldn't use it even for wash water until I cleaned it out.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where'd you haul that water from?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: The city. I had to haul it from the city.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You made a buck a day working for him, but you still used to get by?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah… oh, well I had a little, you see. Roosevelt made it stipulation that any crop you raised when you had a family on 55 acres you could, regardless of mortgage, that's how I had a little money to move on. I took that bunch of oats that I sold, see, I pocketed every load in my pocket. And the banker never said a word.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now this was, you could grow a crop on that guy's place?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh yeah, that is not, that, I'm getting probably too far ahead here. This was in Park, you see, on the doctor's place. Oh, oh, in that place. But I'm trying to tell you that I was allowed that much money, see. I mean, that much crop.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you had some money to live on when you did here?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, oh yeah… oh God yeah, you bet, I wouldn't have moved it. No, no, no, no. And so, then I got this other job and...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You said you, you told Harvey Smith that you wanted to work?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, Harvey Smith, he told this fellow McLean, he says, Ring said you got children going to school. I said, yes sir. Well, he says, McLean, he says, put Ring Sage on. He's got children going to school. He's got a right to have a job. So I got on. There you go then. And I stayed on that winter. And I guess, yeah, that was the summer, and the next summer I got a job down at... Oh, wait a minute, I'll tell you pretty soon. Laird Park. You know, that's down towards Potlatch. I and a guy here in Moscow, we applied for work through the WTAAC. And, no, that was for the Forest Rangers, Forest Service. And got down there and quite a few bunch of, we used to clean that park up see… and..… so then, nobody seemed to be able to file a saw, cross cut saw. And gauge it, you know, and I also had practice enough to learn to file them good.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Make them cut good. So they wanted to know if anybody could do this kind of work. I stuck my neck out, told them I could. They said, you're gonna, that's your job, you gotta file these saws. Well, that's what I did down there that summer. Well then, when I got to with that, along in the fall, I had this old model P I was telling you about. I drove clear to Wenatchee to pick apples for three cents a box. You know where Wenatchee is? I went down there and picked apples for three cents a box, started to. And I knew I couldn't make much that way. So, here come, I was in the past time, and a fella... Had a sign up on the Blackboard, you know, Teamster wanted it… skidding logs… well, gee, I knew all about that. I'd already learnt that up in the woods. And it was five dollars a day and bored. Boy, that was more than I could make of picking apples. I found out where this guy was, and he come in there and I got the job. And it was a heck of a place. It was a mountain, there was shale rock, and the great big yellow pine trees. And boy, you had to know your stuff, and try to figure out how to get them logs out of there without too much work.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: So, I had another partner along with me, another team. And he says, how in the world are you going to get them logs out of that side hill without rolling down the hill? I said, listen buddy, hook your team, your tongs on the back end of that log, and I says, I'll have mine in front here. And I said, you be sure to have them socked in good and tightened up. So, when I go, we both go, and don't give up, keep coming, until we get out to the main trail down the hill… he says, why… i said, boy golly, I know, if you don't, that will go down the hill. It will roll down the hill. Well, it worked.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was he breaking, or was he just following you?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, he just followed you. It was a pretty big log. The two couldn't hardly pull it anyway. It went right along like that. I got out, and so I made a little, well I got by, I got the five dollars a day, but it didn't last too long.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where was this place at anyway?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: This was Wenatchee. Yeah, when I was picking apples.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Wait, tell me one thing here, about what was it like there, and the apple picking at Wenatchee? Was there lots of people there picking?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh yeah, they come from all over, all kinds of people. Yeah, you bet. But, then later years, after that, then I had learned a little how to pick, and cut it in mind, this Ervin Swenson, he wanted to go with me. That was 1928, the year that I got through up here, no wait a minute, that was 1928, now wait a minute to see. Well, that's when I lived in Park, we done that, that's right. We got down there, we got a little more then, though we got, I think it was about five cents a box we got. So we made a little bit better, but you had to board yourself, they had the cabins, see. You boarded yourself, you paid ten cents a day for, they had a cook stove, and slab wood, you burnt, you had to do your own cooking.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you get your own cabin, or did you share a little piece?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, they rented, the orchard had the cabins all over, see, for the pickers.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How many people would live in one cabin?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, it would be different, different orchard had different sized bunches to pick, see. That's what I do. Now this, down there a few years back, now they're doing different, they got, instead of these little hand boxes, they got these great, but you better shut that thing off. Well, I was thinking, I was thinking I should get going and come back another time. Yeah, I believe so.
